record.narrative: I registered a first set of hypothesis-driven comparisons that target biologically interpretable dependencies across all requested outcomes. The strongest expectations are oncogene/pathway addiction and synthetic-lethal axes: KRAS-mutant cells should be more dependent on KRAS; BRAF V600E cells on BRAF; EGFR- or ERBB2-amplified cells on the corresponding receptor; KEAP1-loss cells on NFE2L2; SMARCA4-loss cells on paralog SMARCA2; and MSI-high cells on WRN. I also registered TP53-loss associations with reduced dependency on MDM2 and USP7 because TP53 loss should weaken dependence on p53-regulatory nodes. MYC amplification was used as a broad stress/proliferation predictor for transcription-related dependencies DHX9, POLR2A, RPL11, and mitotic KIF18A. For remaining outcomes, I registered more exploratory pathway-related hypotheses: ERBB2 amplification with STAT3, EGFR amplification with TMED10, and KRAS mutation with RIT1, acknowledging that the RIT1 direction is less certain. All effects will be judged against the 10% relative clinical-significance threshold and uncertainty intervals, with acceptance only if the signed effect and interval support a meaningful difference in this lung cancer dataset.

Selected the 12 claims with the strongest pre-specified biological rationale and direct relevance to the dependency outcomes: oncogene-specific dependencies (KRAS, BRAF, EGFR, ERBB2), canonical synthetic-lethal axes (SMARCA4 loss with SMARCA2; KEAP1 loss with NFE2L2; MSI-high with WRN), TP53-loss attenuation of MDM2 and USP7 dependencies, and MYC amplification as a broad proliferation/transcription-stress predictor for DHX9, RPL11, and POLR2A. Deferred the more exploratory MYC/KIF18A, ERBB2/STAT3, EGFR/TMED10, and KRAS/RIT1 claims until the higher-prior associations are evaluated.

The delivered evidence supports three very large, highly precise dataset-specific associations: SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, TP53 loss is associated with much weaker USP7 dependency, and MSI-high is associated with much stronger WRN dependency. These estimates are far above the 10% relative clinical-significance threshold and their 95% intervals are well away from the null, so I accept them as meaningful associations in this lung cancer cell-line dataset. KEAP1 loss also produced a very large effect, but in the direction opposite to the pre-specified synthetic-lethal expectation: KEAP1-loss samples were less dependent on NFE2L2, not more. I therefore reject the original H6 claim and register a reversed, dataset-specific hypothesis for follow-up. EGFR amplification versus EGFR dependency is borderline: the signed point estimate is just above the 10% threshold, but the interval is close to null, so it remains unresolved and I requested independent validation. KRAS mutation versus KRAS dependency and TP53 loss versus MDM2 dependency have point effects below the threshold with intervals that include both null and possible clinical significance, so they remain unresolved with subgroup follow-up. BRAF V600E and MYC-amplification comparisons for DHX9/RPL11/POLR2A show no support for the expected stronger-dependency direction; H2, H10, H11, and H12 are rejected. ERBB2 amplification is inconclusive and deferred. These are associations in the supplied data, not causal or generalizable claims. The strongest possible concern for the large accepted effects is hidden technical or dataset-design confounding; subgroup and CRISPR-library robustness analyses are proposed to test whether the SMARCA2, USP7, and WRN effects persist across biological and technical strata.

The independent validation for H3 did not upgrade EGFR amplification to an accepted dataset-specific association. R3 gave a borderline signed estimate of +0.0252, just above the approximately 0.0245 absolute clinical-threshold proxy for a 10% difference, with a 95% interval nearly excluding null. However, the independent validation R13 is more informative about generalization within the run: its signed estimate is only +0.0179, below the 10% relative clinical-significance threshold, and its independent interval is wide and includes values consistent with no effect, a clinically meaningful effect, and the opposite direction. The combined discovery-plus-validation pattern is therefore supportive but not sufficiently decisive to accept a scientifically meaningful EGFR amplification effect. I leave H3 unresolved but active because the registered adenocarcinoma subgroup H18 could clarify whether the effect is concentrated in the dominant histologic subtype.

I also reassessed the reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 claim H22. H6 was rejected because the original canonical-direction hypothesis was wrong: KEAP1-loss samples did not have stronger NFE2L2 dependency. Instead, R6 provides very strong evidence in the opposite direction: the signed estimate for H22 is +0.796 with a tight interval entirely away from null, far exceeding the 10% threshold. I therefore accept H22 as a dataset-specific association that KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency in this lung cell-line dataset. This is an observational association, not evidence of general biology or causality, and it may reflect constructed dependencies or technical confounding; robustness checks are needed.

Overall, the strongest supported claims are H5 SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, H8 TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency, H9 MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency, and H22 KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. H2, H6, H10, H11, and H12 remain negative as originally hypothesized, while H1, H3, H4, H7 and some refinements remain unresolved. The next analyses should test whether the large accepted effects survive technical and histologic stratification, especially CRISPR library and adenocarcinoma subtype, and should then request independent validation for the most robust large effects rather than for borderline effects like H3 unless subgroup results strengthen them.

I am now registering refinements that prioritize three tasks: test whether the accepted very large dataset-specific associations are robust to likely technical confounders, test whether borderline unresolved associations can be clarified by more homogeneous or higher-quality subsets, and add biologically motivated class-level or pathway-level predictors where the initial direct-driver hypotheses were weak. The accepted effects for H5, H8, H9, and H22 are so large that they are unlikely to be null, but their interpretability would be harmed if they were driven by low-quality CRISPR screens or a dominant Avana library batch. Therefore, I propose high screen_roc_auc robustness checks for SMARCA2, USP7, WRN, and NFE2L2, and non-Avana library checks for USP7, WRN, and NFE2L2. If these effects remain large and directionally consistent in high-quality or non-Avana strata, I will have more confidence accepting them as dataset-specific associations rather than artifacts. Conversely, attenuation would motivate caution or closure of these robustness investigations.

I also register new biologically motivated comparisons. ARID1A loss is another core SWI/SNF/BAF complex alteration; an association between ARID1A loss and stronger SMARCA2 dependency would suggest that SMARCA2 dependency may be a broader BAF-loss phenotype, while a null result would support greater specificity for SMARCA4 loss. NF1 loss increases RAS-pathway activation and may mimic or modify KRAS-dependent phenotypes; this provides an alternative predictor for KRAS dependency that can help interpret the weak unresolved H1 result. TP53 loss with MDM2 dependency is tested among high Cas9 activity because TP53 loss is biologically expected to weaken MDM2 dependency, but the overall estimate was small; high editing activity reduces one source of screen noise. For EGFR amplification, the adenocarcinoma plus high screen quality subset tests whether the borderline discovery signal was diluted by non-adenocarcinoma samples or lower-quality screens. Finally, the MSI-high WRN association is re-tested among high mutation-burden cells to assess whether the effect is specifically MSI-like rather than merely high mutation burden or replication-stress-related cell state. These proposals remain dataset-specific and observational; they do not imply causality or generalizability.

This analysis request balances broad outcome coverage with focused robustness checks for the currently accepted large dataset-specific associations. First, I selected the four untested direct outcome hypotheses, H13 through H16, so that KIF18A, STAT3, TMED10, and RIT1 receive at least one primary comparison. These are lower-prior exploratory tests, but they are needed to avoid leaving several requested dependency outcomes unexamined. Second, I selected adenocarcinoma-subgroup follow-ups for the four accepted large effects: H19 SMARCA2, H24 USP7, H25 WRN, and H29 NFE2L2. If these very large effects remain large and directionally consistent in the dominant histologic subtype, they are less likely to be driven by the minor non-adenocarcinoma stratum. Third, I selected high-screen-quality follow-ups using screen_roc_auc >= 0.95 for the same four accepted effects: H31, H32, H33, and H34. This tests whether the associations are plausible in higher-confidence CRISPR screens rather than being driven by low-quality screen noise. No claim status is being reassessed in this analyze stage because there are no due validation assessments; these requested analyses will provide new discovery evidence for the next appraise. If the accepted large effects remain robust and exceed the 10% relative clinical-significance threshold, I will consider independent validation for the strongest of them. If subgroup or high-quality analyses show strong attenuation, I will downgrade confidence in biological or technical generalizability within this dataset, while still limiting all conclusions to the supplied data rather than causal claims.

The newly delivered results distinguish two clear groups. First, the accepted large synthetic-lethal-like associations remain extremely robust across both histologic and screen-quality strata. The SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2-dependency effect is approximately +0.777 in adenocarcinoma and +0.790 in higher-quality screens; the TP53-loss USP7-dependency effect is approximately +0.385 and +0.426 in the same strata; the MSI-high WRN-dependency effect is approximately +0.784 and +0.795; and the reversed KEAP1-loss NFE2L2-dependency effect is approximately +0.793 and +0.790. All of these intervals are tight, entirely away from null, and far above any plausible 10% relative clinical-significance threshold for these outcomes. I therefore accept the corresponding refinements H19, H24, H25, H29, H31, H32, H33, and H34 as completed dataset-specific robustness checks and close those specific refinement investigations. These findings do not prove causality or general biology; they show that, within the supplied lung cancer cell-line dataset, the large effects are not restricted to the minor non-adenocarcinoma stratum or to low-quality CRISPR screens. They also do not eliminate possible confounding by correlated genomic or assay features, so later specificity and interaction checks remain useful.

Second, the newly tested exploratory direct hypotheses are mostly weak. H13, MYC amplification with stronger KIF18A dependency, has a very small signed estimate and an interval that includes null but just reaches slightly above a roughly 10% absolute threshold for KIF18A. Because this is a low-prior hypothesis and the point estimate is negligible, I leave it unresolved but defer further work rather than treat it as a meaningful finding. H14, ERBB2 amplification with stronger STAT3 dependency, has a point estimate below the approximate 10% threshold, with an interval that includes both null and clinically possible values; I defer it as inconclusive. H15, EGFR amplification with stronger TMED10 dependency, is also weak and deferral is appropriate. H16, the uncertain KRAS-mutation association with RIT1 dependency, has a small point estimate and an upper 95% bound below the approximate 10% clinical-significance threshold, so I reject it as unsupported in this dataset and close it.

The main critical concern remains multiplicity and post hoc reversal for H22. H22 was registered after observing that the original canonical KEAP1/NFE2L2 direction in H6 was opposite to the observed effect. That makes H22 susceptible to discovery artifact, but the effect is enormous and now appears robust in adenocarcinoma and high-quality screens. Because H22 is the most biologically surprising accepted claim and has not yet received independent validation, I request validation for H22. If it survives independent validation, the dataset-specific claim that KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency will be much more secure. If it fails, I will downgrade H22 to unresolved or reject it despite the original discovery signal. All accepted effects remain limited to this supplied dataset, not causal inference or external generalization.

The independent validation result for H22 is decisive. The original discovery evidence R6 already showed a very large positive signed effect: KEAP1-loss samples had substantially weaker NFE2L2 dependency, not stronger NFE2L2 dependency as the canonical H6 hypothesis predicted. The new validation evidence R26 is even stronger in the same direction, with a signed estimate of approximately +0.810 and an independent 95% interval from about +0.780 to +0.839. This interval remains entirely far above the null and far above any plausible 10% relative clinical-significance threshold for dependency_NFE2L2. The magnitude and consistency across discovery and validation cells substantially reduce the concern that H22 is a discovery-only artifact caused by post hoc reversal, although it still does not prove causality or general biological mechanism. I therefore keep H22 accepted and close this original dataset-specific claim as validated. The shared validation evidence R26 also further supports the rejection of H6: the original canonical-direction hypothesis that KEAP1 loss is associated with stronger NFE2L2 dependency is not supported in this dataset.

The current evidence landscape is now dominated by four validated or highly supported dataset-specific associations: SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, MSI-high status with much stronger WRN dependency, and KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The first three have already survived adenocarcinoma and high-quality-screen stratification; the fourth now has both those robustness checks and independent validation. These remain associations in the supplied lung cancer cell-line dataset, not causal claims or generalizable biological laws. The main remaining scientific uncertainty is whether the strongest effects are partially explained by correlated genomic alterations, co-occurring pathway losses, or assay-technical structure.

The next analysis should therefore focus on specificity and co-alteration independence. For the SMARCA2 effect, it is important to determine whether ARID1A loss, another BAF/SWI-SNF alteration, reproduces the phenotype, and whether SMARCA4 loss remains strong after excluding ARID1A loss. A positive ARID1A result would support a broader BAF-loss phenotype, while specificity for SMARCA4 loss after excluding ARID1A loss would sharpen the interpretation. For USP7, the key follow-up is whether TP53 loss remains associated with weaker USP7 dependency after excluding KEAP1 loss, since KEAP1 loss is another large dataset-specific predictor. For KEAP1/NFE2L2, the reverse validation is strong, but testing KEAP1 loss among TP53-intact lines helps determine whether the effect survives removal of one major correlated genomic predictor. For WRN, MSI-high status is already a huge effect; testing it after excluding TP53 loss and KEAP1 loss assesses whether it is independent of the other accepted predictors. For KRAS, the primary H1 association remains weak, but a co-driver-excluded analysis may clarify whether the small effect is diluted by BRAF, EGFR, or ERBB2 alterations. Finally, combining adenocarcinoma with high screen quality for KEAP1/NFE2L2 and adenocarcinoma with non-Avana library for TP53/USP7 gives compact robustness checks across the most important technical and biological strata simultaneously. The unresolved borderline claims, especially EGFR and KRAS primary associations, should only be promoted if such stratified or specificity analyses produce a clearer signal.

No validation assessments are due at this exploration stage, so I am not changing claim statuses. The current strongest supported dataset-specific associations are H5 SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, H8 TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency, H9 MSI-high status with stronger WRN dependency, and H22 KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. These effects are large enough that the main scientific uncertainty is no longer whether the associations exist in this dataset, but whether their interpretation can be sharpened. I therefore register refinements that test mutual independence among the accepted genomic alterations and assay-quality robustness beyond screen ROC and CRISPR library. The first four proposals restrict each accepted effect to lines that lack the other major accepted co-alterations: SMARCA4 effects are checked among TP53-, KEAP1-, and MSI-negative lines; TP53 effects among KEAP1- and SMARCA4-intact lines; KEAP1 effects among TP53-, SMARCA4-, and MSI-negative lines; and MSI-high WRN effects among TP53-, KEAP1-, and SMARCA4-intact lines. If these remain large, the accepted effects are not easily reduced to a single broad co-alteration phenotype; if they attenuate, the effects should be interpreted more cautiously as composite genomic-state associations rather than isolated gene-marker effects. The next four proposals test all four accepted effects in the high Cas9-activity subset. Screen ROC and library checks reduce broad assay-quality concerns, but Cas9 activity more directly captures editing efficiency; dependence differences driven by noisy or low-editing screens could compress or inflate effects, whereas persistence among high-Cas9 lines would make the associations more credible within this dataset. Finally, I add a biologically motivated WRN-specific follow-up: BRCA2 loss may indicate DNA-repair or replication-stress phenotypes that could extend WRN dependency beyond MSI-high status. Testing BRCA2 loss in high-quality screens, and again in MSI-high-negative lines, evaluates whether WRN dependency is broadly DNA-repair-associated or specifically MSI-associated. All conclusions remain observational associations in the supplied lung cell-line dataset and do not imply causality or external generalizability.

No validation assessments are due, so I am only requesting new analyses. I select the newly registered mutual-independence and editing-efficiency refinements for the four large accepted dataset-specific associations: H51-H54 test each major genomic predictor after excluding other accepted large predictors, and H55-H58 test the same four predictors in the high-Cas9-activity subset. These are higher-value than further subgroup or library checks because the main remaining question is whether the strong effects are specific to individual genomic alterations rather than broad co-alteration or low-quality-screen phenomena. I also select the new WRN/BRCA2 analyses H59-H60 to test whether WRN dependency is specifically MSI-associated or broadly related to DNA-repair/replication-stress markers. Finally, I select H43-H44 for the SMARCA2/BAF specificity check: H43 tests ARID1A loss among SMARCA4-intact lines, while H44 tests SMARCA4 loss among ARID1A-intact lines. If H43 is positive, the SMARCA2 phenotype may reflect a broader BAF-loss class effect; if H43 is null while H44 remains large, SMARCA4-specific interpretation is strengthened. This batch therefore prioritizes specificity, independence, and technical robustness of the strongest findings rather than retesting already well-supported robustness strata.

All reported estimates are signed to the hypothesis direction, so positive signed estimates support the stated association. The new mutual-exclusion refinements H51 through H54 show that the four large accepted effects remain large after removing other major accepted co-alterations: SMARCA4-loss-associated stronger SMARCA2 dependency remains approximately +0.784 when excluding TP53-, KEAP1-, and MSI-negative lines; TP53-loss-associated weaker USP7 dependency remains approximately +0.397 when excluding KEAP1 and SMARCA4 lines; KEAP1-loss-associated weaker NFE2L2 dependency remains approximately +0.794 when excluding TP53-, SMARCA4-, and MSI-negative lines; and MSI-high-associated stronger WRN dependency remains approximately +0.770 when excluding TP53-, KEAP1-, and SMARCA4-intact confounders, despite a smaller exposed cell count of 62. The high-Cas9-activity refinements H55 through H58 similarly remain large and directionally stable. I therefore accept and close these as completed within-dataset specificity and editing-quality robustness checks. These are not causal or generalization claims, but they reduce the concern that the accepted effects are explained solely by broad co-alteration states or by low-Cas9-activity screens. The BAF specificity check is particularly informative: H44 accepts/closes because the SMARCA4-loss effect remains approximately +0.777 among ARID1A-intact lines, whereas H43 rejects/closes because ARID1A loss among SMARCA4-intact lines has a near-null signed estimate and an upper interval bound below a plausible 10% relative benchmark for this outcome. This supports SMARCA4-specific SMARCA2 dependency in this dataset more than a generic ARID1A-loss effect. The BRCA2-WRN checks H59 and H60 are not clinically decisive in either direction: the point estimates are essentially null and intervals cross zero, but the upper signed bounds for WRN are roughly +0.049 and +0.044, which could exceed a 10% relative threshold depending on comparator mean. Because they do not show positive evidence and are not low-priority equivalence questions, I leave them unresolved and deferred rather than rejecting as null. For H8, the accepted USP7 effect is now supported across adenocarcinoma, high screen ROC, mutual exclusion, and high Cas9-activity strata, but its magnitude is smaller than the other accepted huge effects and the biological direction is surprising. Therefore it is the best current target for independent validation. I request validation for H8. I also reassess H5 and H9 as still-active accepted primary effects with updated robustness evidence, and reassess H3 as unresolved/deferred because the EGFR discovery association was borderline and independent validation did not provide confirmation.

All estimates below are already signed to the corresponding hypothesis direction, so a positive signed estimate supports the registered association. The newly delivered validation evidence changes the conclusion for two major claims and leaves one borderline claim unresolved.

First, H8 is now independently validated. Discovery R8 gave a signed effect of approximately +0.396 (95% interval about +0.325 to +0.467), and validation R39 gives a signed effect of approximately +0.434 with an independent interval about +0.329 to +0.539. Relative to the typical magnitude of dependency_USP7 scores around the comparator mean, this is far above the approximately 10% relative-effect benchmark used for this task. The validation result is also larger in the same direction as discovery, so I accept H8 and close its primary investigation. Scientifically, within this supplied dataset, TP53-loss lines show much weaker USP7 dependency, meaning their USP7 scores are less negative than those of TP53-intact lines. This is an observational association, not a causal claim or a claim of external generalizability, but the independent confirmation plus the earlier adenocarcinoma, high-screen-ROC, high-Cas9, and co-alteration-exclusion robustness results make it one of the better-supported dataset-specific findings.

Second, H31 is validated in the high-screen-ROC stratum. R40 has a signed effect of approximately +0.812 with an independent interval about +0.773 to +0.851. This confirms that the SMARCA4-loss association with stronger SMARCA2 dependency is not restricted to lower-quality screens or the overall population. I accept H31 and close it as a completed robustness refinement. This indirectly strengthens H5, though H5 itself remains accepted without direct independent validation of the unstratified primary comparison. H5 remains active because, if additional validation resources are available, direct independent validation of the primary SMARCA2 association would be a clean final robustness step. The evidence now supports a dataset-specific claim that SMARCA4-loss lines have markedly stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and this effect is not explained by broader ARID1A loss because H44 showed persistence among ARID1A-intact lines while H43 showed that ARID1A loss among SMARCA4-intact lines is negligible.

Third, H3 remains unresolved after validation. Discovery R3 showed a borderline positive signed association of EGFR amplification with stronger EGFR dependency, with estimate about +0.025 and interval just crossing null. Validation R13 gives a smaller signed estimate of about +0.018 with a wide independent interval from about -0.028 to +0.064. The validation point estimate is below the approximate 10% relative benchmark and does not confirm a clinically meaningful difference. I therefore keep H3 unresolved and deferred rather than accepting it as a meaningful association. This is not a strong null claim because the upper interval could still cover a modest clinically meaningful effect, but the current evidence does not justify acceptance.

The overall scientific picture is dominated by four supported dataset-specific associations. SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency (H5 accepted, with H31 now independently validated in high-quality screens). TP53 loss is associated with much weaker USP7 dependency (H8 accepted and now independently validated). MSI-high status is associated with much stronger WRN dependency (H9 accepted, with adenocarcinoma, high-ROC, high-Cas9, and co-alteration-exclusion robustness, though primary independent validation has not yet been completed). KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency (H22 accepted and independently validated), which directly opposes the canonical stronger-dependency hypothesis H6, now rejected/closed. These are not causal claims; the associations could reflect correlated genomic structure, cell-line lineage effects, or other unmeasured features. However, the mutual-exclusion and quality-stratification analyses argue against simple explanations based only on low screen quality, low Cas9 activity, broad co-alteration states, or the minor non-adenocarcinoma stratum.

Negative or non-supported findings include: BRAF V600E association with stronger BRAF dependency (H2 rejected), canonical KEAP1 stronger NFE2L2 dependency (H6 rejected), MYC amplification with stronger DHX9/RPL11/POLR2A dependency (H10-H12 rejected), KRAS mutation with altered RIT1 dependency (H16 rejected), and ARID1A loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency among SMARCA4-intact lines (H43 rejected). These negative results are useful because they narrow interpretation, especially the BAF-pathway specificity: the large SMARCA2 effect tracks with SMARCA4 loss rather than with ARID1A loss in this dataset.

Unresolved or low-confidence signals include the KRAS and EGFR driver-marker primary comparisons, several MYC/RTK-associated weak dependencies, MDM2-TP53, and WRN-BRCA2 extensions. The WRN-BRCA2 results do not currently support a broad DNA-repair extension of MSI-driven WRN dependency, but the intervals are not tight enough for definitive rejection. The most informative next analyses should focus on either completing independent validation for the still-unvalidated large accepted effects, especially H9 and possibly H5, or closing the remaining weak driver-marker hypotheses using high-quality and lineage-specific strata. I have registered one new high-quality adenocarcinoma ERBB2 follow-up to allow a focused closure or upgrade decision for that weak RTK-amplification signal. The next analysis batch should prioritize H62 and H61 for full co-alteration specificity, H48 for KRAS co-driver-excluded dependency_KRAS, H41 and the new ERBB2 refinement for driver amplification dependencies, H40 for TP53-MDM2 under high Cas9, and H42 for WRN under higher mutation burden.

No validation assessments are due, so the registered scientific conclusions are unchanged. The strongest supported within-dataset associations remain SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, MSI-high status with much stronger WRN dependency, and KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency. These remain observational associations in the supplied lung cell-line dataset, not causal claims or generalizable biological rules. The next analysis should therefore sharpen the accepted effects and resolve only the most informative weak signals. I register five new high-value proposals. First, NF1 loss among KRAS-wild-type lines versus dependency_KRAS tests whether upstream RAS-pathway activation, rather than KRAS mutation specifically, associates with stronger KRAS dependency; the alternative is that KRAS dependency is governed by isoform-specific context or bypass biology. Second, KRAS mutation versus dependency_KRAS among high Cas9 activity reduces editing-noise in the weak primary KRAS association and asks whether a small effect becomes clearer when screens are most efficient. Third, ERBB2 amplification versus dependency_STAT3 among adenocarcinoma lines with high screen ROC tests whether a weak RTK-related signal is biologically coherent in the most informative lineage and highest-quality screens; the alternative is a null pathway association. Fourth, TP53 loss versus dependency_MDM2 among high screen ROC evaluates the MDM2 hypothesis in a high-quality stratum where the observed MDM2 standard deviation could allow a 10%-relative difference to be detected. Fifth, SMARCA4 loss versus dependency_POLR2A is a specificity check for the huge SMARCA4 loss effect: if SMARCA4 loss creates a broad transcription/BAF vulnerability, POLR2A dependency may also increase; if the effect is SMARCA2-specific, POLR2A should remain near null. I also defer many lower-priority active library, lineage, or redundant exclusion follow-ups so that the next analyze step can focus on full co-alteration specificity, driver-marker refinements, and the newly registered high-value tests.

No assessments are due at this stage, so I am only selecting previously registered analyses. I prioritize the most informative remaining questions: (1) full co-alteration specificity of the two strongest non-validated large effects, H61 for SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 dependency and H62 for TP53-loss USP7 dependency; (2) new driver/RAS pathway refinements, H48 for KRAS dependency after excluding major co-drivers, H64 for NF1 loss among KRAS-wild-type lines, and H65 for KRAS mutation in high Cas9 activity; (3) high-quality driver-marker closures for EGFR, ERBB2, STAT3, and MDM2, H41, H63, H66, H67, and H40; (4) WRN biology beyond MSI-high status, H42 under higher mutation burden; and (5) pathway specificity of the SMARCA4 loss effect, H68 SMARCA4 loss versus POLR2A dependency. This batch avoids reusing already tested low-priority library or lineage strata and focuses on resolving whether accepted effects are marker-specific and whether weak driver-marker signals become meaningful in high-quality biological strata.

All new discovery estimates are signed to the hypothesis direction, so positive signed estimates support the registered association. First, the strongest accepted effects are further reinforced by full co-alteration and mutation-burden refinements. H62 remains very large: TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency among KEAP1-intact, SMARCA4-intact, MSI-stable lines, signed +0.422, interval +0.331 to +0.513. This is far above the approximate 10% relative benchmark for dependency_USP7. I accept and close H62 as a completed mutual-independence robustness refinement. H61 similarly remains very large: SMARCA4 loss is associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency after excluding ARID1A-, TP53-, KEAP1-, and MSI-associated lines, signed +0.780, interval +0.753 to +0.806. I accept and close H61. H42 shows MSI-high-associated stronger WRN dependency in higher-mutation-burden lines, signed +0.786, interval +0.754 to +0.818, which is also huge relative to the WRN scale; I accept and close H42. These refinements argue against simple co-alteration or low-mutation-burden explanations for the major accepted associations. Second, the KRAS results remain weak or directionally inconsistent. H65 shows positive evidence in the high-Cas9 stratum, signed +0.030, interval +0.004 to +0.056. The point estimate is above the rough 10% relative benchmark for dependency_KRAS, but the lower bound is well below it, so I leave H65 unresolved and active rather than accepting a modest driver-marker claim. H48, testing KRAS mutation among lines without BRAF, EGFR, or ERBB2 alterations, has signed +0.013 with interval -0.007 to +0.033; this is underpowered/weak and remains unresolved and deferred. H64 is different: among KRAS-wild-type lines, NF1 loss gives a significant signed estimate of -0.039, interval -0.071 to -0.006, meaning raw KRAS dependency is less negative in NF1-loss lines, i.e. weaker rather than stronger dependency. Therefore the original claim H64 is rejected and closed; the opposite association is potentially interesting but post hoc, so I register a reversed claim for later testing rather than immediately accepting it. Third, the weak driver-marker and pathway-specific hypotheses mostly do not support meaningful associations. H41, H63, H66, and H40 all have intervals crossing null and point estimates below or only marginally near a 10% relative benchmark, so they remain unresolved and deferred. H67 is more decisive against TP53 loss increasing MDM2 dependency in the high-screen-ROC stratum: signed estimate -0.013, interval -0.048 to +0.021, with the upper bound below the rough 10% threshold for dependency_MDM2; I reject and close H67. H68 supports specificity of the SMARCA4 loss phenotype because SMARCA4 loss is not associated with stronger POLR2A dependency: signed estimate -0.005, interval -0.024 to +0.014, with the positive-side upper bound below the 10% benchmark for POLR2A; I reject and close H68. Fourth, I request independent validation for H9. H9, MSI-high status associated with much stronger WRN dependency, is one of the largest accepted within-dataset associations but has not yet received direct independent validation, unlike H8, H22, and H31. Validation is not required for acceptance, but it is the most useful current validation target for the primary accepted set.

All estimates below are already signed to the registered hypothesis direction, so a positive signed estimate supports the corresponding claim. Two evidence items must be assessed at synthesis: the H22 response deadline and the new independent validation of H9.

H22, KEAP1 loss associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, is strongly and independently confirmed. Discovery R6 gave a signed estimate of about +0.796 with interval about +0.776 to +0.816; independent validation R26 gives about +0.810 with independent interval about +0.780 to +0.839. On the dependency scale, this is far larger than the approximate 10% relative-effect benchmark and the validation interval remains entirely on the same side. I therefore accept H22 and keep its investigation closed. The canonical claim H6, KEAP1 loss associated with stronger NFE2L2 dependency, remains rejected and closed because the opposite direction is supported in both discovery and validation.

The overall supported dataset-specific core remains: SMARCA4 loss is associated with markedly stronger dependency_SMARCA2 in broad and multiple constrained contexts; KEAP1 loss is associated with markedly weaker dependency_NFE2L2; TP53 loss is associated with markedly weaker dependency_USP7, including validated contexts; MSI-high status is associated with markedly stronger dependency_WRN; and PTEN loss is associated with stronger dependency_STAT3 across broad and several accepted contexts, now including high screen quality/high Cas9, TP53-loss, high-EMT, high-IFN main effect, high stemness, and other constrained settings. Negative or unsupported signals remain broad: KRAS mutation does not show a clinically meaningful full-population effect on dependency_KRAS; BRAF V600E does not show a meaningful effect on dependency_BRAF, including KRAS-wild-type lines; EGFR amplification does not show a meaningful dependency_EGFR or dependency_TMED10 effect; ERBB2 amplification does not show a meaningful dependency_ERBB2 or dependency_STAT3 effect; MYC amplification lacks broad clinically meaningful effects on dependency_DHX9, dependency_RPL11, dependency_POLR2A, and dependency_KIF18A; TP53 loss does not show a clinically meaningful canonical MDM2 dependency effect; validation does not support a stable PTEN-loss effect on dependency_KRAS among KRAS-mutant lines; MSI-high does not support dependency_POLR2A after validation; and the constructed research markers D/E/F do not provide clinically meaningful signals for the tested outcomes. The most informative next analyses are interaction and complement tests for effect modification of the accepted PTEN-loss/STAT3 and TP53-loss/USP7 associations: low-IFN-gamma complement main effect for PTEN loss/STAT3, high-EMT interaction for PTEN loss/STAT3, and high-AXL interaction for TP53 loss/USP7. These are observational within the supplied dataset and do not establish causality, mechanism, or external generalizability.

No assessments are due, so I do not change any existing claim statuses. I register a new set of falsifiable follow-up comparisons rather than refinements, to avoid missing motivating-evidence links and to broaden the evidence base around accepted dataset-specific associations. The WRN proposals ask whether the accepted MSI-high association remains strong in technically stringent screens with mutation burden below the top quartile, and whether it persists in TP53-loss lines. The first would support an MSI-context effect rather than a generic mutation-burden proxy; the second would test whether p53 context coexists with, rather than explains, the MSI signal. The STAT3 proposals test PTEN-loss-associated stronger STAT3 dependency in technically stringent low-IFN-gamma lines, high-MYC-expression lines, and high-AXL-expression lines. These probe whether the broad PTEN-loss/STAT3 association is robust in expression contexts with potentially distinct transcriptional, RTK, inflammatory, or Cas9-quality biology. The KRAS/receptor proposals test pathway-bypass specificity: among KRAS-wild-type high-quality lines, BRAF V600E is expected to show weaker KRAS dependency if downstream activation bypasses KRAS, while EGFR amplification is expected to show stronger KRAS dependency if upstream receptor signaling feeds through RAS. Conversely, among KRAS-mutant lines, EGFR and ERBB2 dependency should be weaker if KRAS mutation bypasses those receptor nodes. The NFE2L2 proposal tests whether the accepted KEAP1-loss-associated weaker dependency persists in TP53-loss lines, where co-loss may change oxidative-stress and p53-associated survival biology. The non-Avana high-quality robustness tests ask whether the very strong SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 and TP53-loss/USP7 associations survive in screens with a different library, controlling for high screen ROC quality. I use approximate 10% population-scale dependency-score benchmarks for each outcome. For dependency_STAT3 and dependency_USP7, a benchmark is about 0.028; for dependency_KRAS, dependency_EGFR, dependency_BRAF, and dependency_WRN, about 0.025-0.030; for dependency_SMARCA2 and dependency_NFE2L2, the effects are expected to be very large if real. A proposal will be considered scientifically meaningful only if the signed estimate and lower interval bound support the registered direction near or above these thresholds. All claims remain observational within the supplied dataset and are not interpreted as causal or generalizable.

No assessments are due, so I change no existing claim statuses. I select 12 previously registered, currently active, and currently unevaluated comparisons that provide the highest-value follow-up from the current evidence. I avoid rerunning H149 because its interaction result is already available and rerunning it would not provide new sample. The selected set tests three priorities. First, it probes effect modification and complement contexts around the accepted PTEN-loss/STAT3 and TP53-loss/USP7 associations: H150 gives the low-IFN complement main effect needed to interpret the high-IFN interaction; H151 tests the high-EMT interaction after validated attenuation of the high-EMT main effect; H152 tests whether high AXL expression modifies TP53-loss-associated USP7 dependency; H154 tests the PTEN-loss/STAT3 association under stringent low-IFN screening conditions. Second, it tests MAPK pathway bypass specificity: H157 and H158 ask whether KRAS dependency in KRAS-wild-type high-quality screens is altered by BRAF V600E or EGFR amplification, while H159 and H160 ask whether EGFR or ERBB2 dependency is weaker among KRAS-mutant lines as expected if KRAS mutation bypasses receptor nodes. Third, it tests robustness of accepted stress-response and assay-context associations: H153 asks whether the MSI-high/WRN association remains strong when mutation burden is below the top quartile, H161 asks whether KEAP1-loss-associated weaker NFE2L2 persists in TP53-loss lines, and H163/H164 ask whether the very strong SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 and TP53-loss/USP7 associations survive non-Avana library screens with high screen quality. I deferred H155/H156 because the PTEN-loss/STAT3 association is already broad and many context tests have been done, and deferred H162 because the MSI-high/TP53-loss intersection may be underpowered. Returned intervals are already signed to each registered direction, so positive signed values support the registered hypothesis. I will interpret meaningful effects against the approximate 10% population-scale benchmark, about +0.025 to +0.030 absolute dependency-score units for KRAS/EGFR/ERBB2/BRAF/WRN/STAT3/USP7-type outcomes, while judging small-cell and context-dependent claims cautiously. All conclusions remain observational within the supplied dataset.

All intervals are already signed to the registered direction, so positive values support the claim. I used approximate 10% population-scale absolute dependency-score benchmarks for acceptance: roughly +0.028 for STAT3-type effects, +0.025 to +0.026 for KRAS/EGFR/ERBB2-type effects, +0.030 for WRN, and +0.017 to +0.018 for USP7; very large effects were accepted when the lower bound was far above benchmark. H150 and H154 accept strongly: PTEN loss is associated with much stronger dependency_STAT3 in the low-IFN complement and in technically stringent low-IFN screens, with signed lower bounds +0.152 and +0.098 respectively, well above benchmark. These are robust dataset-specific context associations, not causal claims. H153 accepts: the MSI-high dependency_WRN association remains very strong even in high-quality screens with mutation burden below the top quartile, lower bound +0.761, supporting an MSI context rather than a generic mutation-burden proxy. H161 accepts: the KEAP1-loss-associated weaker NFE2L2 dependency persists in TP53-loss lines, lower bound +0.763. H163 accepts the very strong SMARCA4-loss-associated dependency_SMARCA2 effect in non-Avana high-quality screens, lower bound +0.690, despite modest cell counts. H151 and H152 are unresolved but deferred: the high-EMT PTEN-loss STAT3 interaction and high-AXL TP53-loss USP7 interaction have large point estimates but signed lower bounds of only +0.011 and +0.008, below clinically meaningful thresholds. They may reflect effect modification, but multiplicity, subgroup selection, and dependence on discovery-only interaction estimates prevent acceptance. H157 is unresolved and closed because the BRAF V600E effect on dependency_KRAS in KRAS-wild-type high-quality screens is near null with broad uncertainty. H158 and H160 reject the registered positive directions: EGFR amplification does not support clinically meaningful stronger dependency_KRAS in KRAS-wild-type screens, and ERBB2 amplification does not support clinically meaningful stronger dependency_ERBB2 among KRAS mutants; signed upper bounds fall below the relevant benchmarks. H159 rejects the registered positive direction but the signed interval is entirely negative and clinically meaningful in the opposite direction, suggesting EGFR amplification may be associated with stronger dependency_EGFR among KRAS mutants in this dataset. Because this reversal was discovered after seeing the wrong-signed original interaction and has no independent validation, I did not accept it automatically; I registered a new reversed proposal as unresolved and parented it to H159. H164 is unresolved and closed because the non-Avana high-quality TP53-loss USP7 signal is underpowered, with an interval crossing zero. H149 is left status unresolved but investigation closed: the reversed high-IFN interaction has a strong discovery interval, but validation of the high-IFN main effect was attenuated, and independent confirmation of the interaction is lacking. No validation was requested because no new validation requests remain. All conclusions remain observational within the supplied dataset and do not establish causality or generalizability.

All intervals are already signed to the registered hypothesis direction, so positive signed values support the registered direction. H123 now has independent validation. For PTEN-loss versus PTEN-intact lines with high IFN-gamma signature, the discovery signed association with stronger dependency_STAT3 was +0.423 (interval +0.319 to +0.527). The independent adjusted validation signed effect was +0.193 with lower bound +0.045 and upper bound +0.340. Using the approximate 10% population-scale benchmark for STAT3 of about +0.028, the validated lower bound is above the clinical-meaningfulness threshold, so I accept and close H123. The validation effect is materially attenuated relative to discovery, which is consistent with some context inflation in the high-IFN-gamma discovery estimate, but the independent interval still supports a scientifically meaningful dataset-specific PTEN-loss/STAT3 association in that context. I am closing H151 and H152 as unresolved because their signed lower bounds (+0.011 and +0.008, respectively) are below the relevant 10% benchmarks and validation requests are exhausted. I am also closing H165 as unresolved because the reversed EGFR-amplification/KRAS-mutant EGFR-dependency signal is post hoc and the lower bound is too close to zero for confident acceptance. The supported dataset-specific core remains: SMARCA4 loss is associated with markedly stronger SMARCA2 dependency; KEAP1 loss is associated with markedly weaker NFE2L2 dependency; TP53 loss is associated with markedly weaker USP7 dependency; MSI-high status is associated with markedly stronger WRN dependency; and PTEN loss is associated with stronger STAT3 dependency across broad and several constrained contexts, now including the validated high-IFN-gamma context. Negative or unsupported findings include clinically meaningful null results for most receptor/MAPK and MYC-amplification hypotheses, no canonical TP53-loss/MDM2 effect, no stable PTEN-loss effect on KRAS dependency among KRAS-mutant lines, no supported MSI-high effect on POLR2A, and no meaningful constructed-marker effects. The most informative next analyses are robustness checks in technically stringent screens for the accepted PTEN-loss/STAT3 contexts (high IFN, high EMT, and high stemness) and for TP53-loss/USP7 in high AXL expression, while retaining active complement/context tests for PTEN-loss/STAT3 under high MYC or high AXL and MSI-high/WRN under TP53 loss. All conclusions remain observational within the supplied dataset and do not establish causality or generalizability.

No assessments are due, so I do not change any existing claim statuses. I registered twelve new comparisons aimed at two goals: robustness of the accepted dataset-specific associations under additional biological and technical contexts, and follow-up of one still-ambiguous RB1/KIF18A pathway signal. For accepted associations, returned estimates are already signed to the registered direction, so positive values support the registered hypothesis. The main alternative explanations I consider are context-specific attenuation, multiplicity/subgroup selection, technical confounding, or small-cell instability. I avoid stacking multiple stringent QC filters in rare-exposure contexts because that can make exposed cells fall below 20; instead each context uses either high Cas9 activity or high screen ROC plus a slow-growth context. The STAT3 proposals ask whether PTEN-loss-associated stronger dependency_STAT3 remains clinically meaningful in high interferon, EMT, stemness, MYC, AXL, and high-serum contexts. The USP7 proposals ask whether TP53-loss-associated weaker USP7 dependency remains in high AXL and high MYC contexts. The SMARCA2 proposal asks whether the very strong SMARCA4-loss signal remains in high-quality slow-growing screens, reducing concern that the signal is driven by fast-growing lines or screening quality. The NFE2L2 proposals ask whether the strong KEAP1-loss-associated weaker NFE2L2 dependency persists in high-interferon and high-quality slow-growing contexts. The RB1 proposal retests RB1-loss-associated dependency_KIF18A under combined high screen quality and high Cas9 activity, because the earlier screen-quality-only result was directionally favorable but not decisive. I will judge acceptance against approximate 10% population-scale thresholds for the outcome: about 0.028 for dependency_STAT3, 0.018 for dependency_USP7, 0.042 for dependency_SMARCA2, 0.009 for dependency_NFE2L2, 0.026 for dependency_KIF18A, and about 0.030 for dependency_WRN. Effects with point estimates but lower bounds below these thresholds will remain unresolved rather than accepted, and all conclusions remain observational within the supplied dataset, not causal or necessarily generalizable.

No assessments are due, so I make no status changes to existing claims. I request 12 previously registered, currently unevaluated analyses selected for high scientific value. H100 is a priority interaction: PTEN loss showed a positive discovery association with dependency_KRAS in KRAS-mutant lines in H89, but independent validation reversed that result; H100 directly tests whether the PTEN-loss effect differs by KRAS-mutation status. H162 tests whether the accepted very strong MSI-high/dependency_WRN association persists within TP53-loss lines, though the exposed cell is likely near the minimum and will be interpreted cautiously. For PTEN-loss/STAT3, I request high-quality-screen context main effects for AXL-high H156, high IFN H166, high EMT H167, and high stemness H168, complementing the broadly accepted PTEN-loss/STAT3 association and the validated but attenuated high-IFN effect. For TP53-loss/USP7, I request high AXL with high screen quality H169, high AXL with high Cas9 H175, and high MYC with high Cas9 H176, because TP53-loss/USP7 is accepted broadly but AXL showed an unresolved interaction. I also request robustness/follow-up tests for SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 in slow-growing high-quality screens H177, KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in high IFN with high Cas9 H178, and the ambiguous RB1-loss/dependency_KIF18A signal under high screen quality and high Cas9 H179. Returned intervals will already be signed to the registered direction, so positive signed values support the registered hypothesis; acceptance will require lower bounds to exceed outcome-specific approximate 10% population-scale benchmarks, and small-cell context estimates will be handled conservatively. No validation can be requested because voluntary validation requests are exhausted. All conclusions will remain observational within this supplied dataset and will not be treated as causal or generally reproducible unless supported.

All returned intervals are already signed to the registered hypothesis direction, so positive signed values support the registered direction. I used approximate 10% population-scale absolute dependency-score benchmarks for acceptance: about 0.028 for STAT3, 0.018 for USP7, 0.026 for KIF18A, 0.030 for WRN, 0.042 for SMARCA2, 0.009 for NFE2L2, and 0.025 to 0.030 for KRAS/BRAF/EGFR/ERBB2-type scores. Acceptance required a valid lower bound above the relevant benchmark and sufficient consistency with prior evidence. H100 remains unresolved and closed: the PTEN-loss/KRAS-mutant interaction on dependency_KRAS is positive (+0.066), but its signed lower bound is only +0.016, below the KRAS benchmark, and it conflicts with the failed independent validation of the simpler PTEN-loss-in-KRAS-mutant main effect H89. This is suggestive of possible effect modification but not clinically meaningful with uncertainty, and no validation remains. H156, H166, H167, and H168 are accepted as dataset-specific context associations: PTEN loss is associated with clinically stronger dependency_STAT3 in high-quality screens with high AXL, high IFN-gamma, high EMT, or high stemness, with signed lower bounds +0.086, +0.185, +0.164, and +0.115 respectively, all well above the STAT3 benchmark. These are observational subgroup associations and may be context-specific or influenced by selection on measured features. H162 is accepted despite an exposed cell of 24 because the MSI-high dependency_WRN association within TP53-loss lines is extremely strong, signed lower bound +0.765, far above the WRN benchmark; it supports persistence of the MSI/WRN signal in a TP53-loss context rather than a TP53-loss-specific effect. H169, H175, and H176 are accepted: TP53 loss is associated with clinically weaker dependency_USP7 in high AXL and high MYC contexts under technical QC, with signed lower bounds +0.165, +0.109, and +0.257, all far above the USP7 benchmark. These are consistent with the broad TP53-loss/USP7 association, although the earlier AXL interaction H152 was not itself decisive. H177 and H178 are accepted: SMARCA4 loss remains very strongly associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency in slow-growing high-quality screens (lower +0.752), and KEAP1 loss remains very strongly associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency in high IFN-gamma/high Cas9 screens (lower +0.713). Both have small exposed cells but enormous effects. H179 remains unresolved and closed: RB1 loss in high-quality/high-Cas9 screens gives a near-zero signed estimate for dependency_KIF18A, interval -0.057 to +0.052, which is too imprecise to support the registered direction and too wide to rule out a clinically meaningful effect. No validation was requested because voluntary validation requests are exhausted. All conclusions remain observational within the supplied lung-line dataset and do not establish causality or generalizability.

I reassessed the due validation for H132 and accept it as a supported, dataset-specific association. The claim tests whether PTEN loss is associated with a more negative, i.e. stronger, dependency_STAT3 score among lines with high EMT score (emt_score >= 0.66). Returned estimates are already signed to the negative claim direction, so positive values support the claim. The discovery estimate was +0.378 (95% Welch interval +0.261 to +0.495), and the independent validation estimate was +0.262 (adjusted interval +0.084 to +0.441). The validation is meaningfully attenuated, but its lower bound still exceeds the approximate 10% population-scale STAT3 benchmark of about 0.028 used in this run and remains far from null. Therefore I accept and close H132, while noting that the smaller validation estimate suggests some discovery-context inflation and that the inference remains observational within the supplied lung-line dataset.

Final synthesis of the run so far: the strongest, repeatedly supported dataset-specific associations are (1) SMARCA4 loss is associated with markedly stronger SMARCA2 dependency, robust across global, adenocarcinoma, high screen quality, high Cas9 activity, low-growth, MYC-high, PTEN-loss, and ARID1A-loss contexts; (2) KEAP1 loss is associated with markedly weaker/less-negative NFE2L2 dependency, with discovery and independent validation concordant and robust across multiple contexts; (3) TP53 loss is associated with markedly weaker USP7 dependency, validated and reproducible in broad and several QC/biology-restricted contexts; (4) MSI-high is associated with markedly stronger WRN dependency, validated and robust including within high-quality, TP53-loss, and mutation-burden-selected settings; and (5) PTEN loss is associated with stronger STAT3 dependency, supported broadly, through multiple technical and biological contexts, and validated in high-IFN-gamma and high-EMT settings. H132 adds an independently validated high-EMT PTEN-loss/STAT3 context, albeit with attenuation relative to discovery.

Negative or unsupported findings include clinically meaningful null results for most direct receptor-tyrosine-kinase amplification effects on their own dependency scores: BRAF V600E did not support dependency_BRAF; EGFR amplification did not produce a robust self-dependency effect; ERBB2 amplification was near-null for dependency_ERBB2 and dependency_STAT3. MYC amplification did not support dependency_DHX9, dependency_RPL11, dependency_POLR2A, or dependency_KIF18A. Canonical TP53 loss did not show a stable clinically meaningful MDM2-dependency effect, and several technical QC-restricted follow-ups were null or small. RB1 loss remained unresolved for dependency_KIF18A, with near-zero or imprecise estimates. PTEN loss did not show a stable effect on dependency_KRAS among KRAS-mutant lines: the discovery-positive but validation-reversed H89 and the unresolved interaction H100 do not support a clinically meaningful KRAS-dependency modification. MSI-high had no supported effect on dependency_POLR2A after validation, and the constructed research markers D/E/F showed only small near-null associations.

The main unresolved uncertainty is whether several accepted context effects are context-specific or selected by the measured feature filters, especially in small exposed cells with strong screen-quality or expression-based eligibility filters. Multiplicity is substantial, and although validation intervals were wide because they accounted for the maximum number of validations, many accepted effects have very large lower bounds. The evidence establishes associations within this supplied dataset, not causality, therapeutic synthetic lethality, or generalizability outside these lung-line measurements.

Most informative next analyses are to evaluate the currently active claims that test accepted associations under additional high-Cas9 contexts: H170-H174 for PTEN-loss/STAT3 under high IFN, EMT, stemness, MYC, and AXL with high Cas9 activity; H155 for PTEN-loss/STAT3 under high-quality MYC-high screens; H180 for PTEN-loss/STAT3 under high serum with high Cas9; and H181 for KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 in slow-growing high-quality screens. If their signed lower bounds exceed the outcome-specific 10% benchmarks, they can add robustness or new accepted contexts; if lower bounds fall below benchmarks, the broader accepted effects should still stand but those narrower biological contexts should remain unresolved rather than accepted.
